problemText: Earth's atmosphere is divided into four main layers. Name the layer that extends from the ground to approximately 12 kilometers in altitude.
choices: Thermosphere
Stratosphere
Mesosphere
Troposphere
hints: This is the lowest layer, where weather and clouds occur.
The name comes from 'tropo-' meaning turning or changing, matching the weather in this layer.

problemText: A weather balloon carries instruments high into the atmosphere. From ground level, the instruments measure that temperature drops steadily as the balloon rises. At what altitude will this steady temperature drop stop, and what change in temperature trend should the instruments detect at that point?
choices: At about 12 kilometers, where temperature will start to rise instead of fall
At about 50 kilometers, where temperature will start to rise instead of fall
At about 85 kilometers, where temperature will start to fall even faster
At about 400 kilometers, where temperature will level off and stay constant
hints: The boundary between two layers marks a reversal in how temperature changes with altitude.
The troposphere's upper limit is where the air stops getting colder the higher you go.

problemText: By volume, Earth's atmosphere is composed mainly of two gases. These two gases together make up about 99 percent of dry air. Nitrogen accounts for about 78 percent, so what percentage of the atmosphere does oxygen make up?
choices: About 1 percent
About 21 percent
About 12 percent
About 50 percent
hints: Add the two percentages: they must equal about 99 percent total.
If one gas is 78 percent and the total of both is 99 percent, subtract to find the other.

problemText: A research aircraft climbs from sea level through the stratosphere and into the mesosphere. The pilot notes that as the plane climbed from 30 kilometers to 70 kilometers altitude, the temperature outside first increased, then decreased. Based on the altitude ranges and temperature trends of the layers, explain which two layers the plane passed through during this climb and why the temperature trend changed between them.
choices: The plane passed through the troposphere then the stratosphere; temperature stopped falling and started rising when the plane crossed from the troposphere into the stratosphere at about 12 kilometers
The plane passed through the mesosphere then the thermosphere; temperature stopped falling and started rising when the plane crossed from the mesosphere into the thermosphere at about 85 kilometers
The plane passed through the stratosphere then the mesosphere; temperature stopped rising and started falling when the plane crossed from the stratosphere into the mesosphere at about 50 kilometers
The plane stayed in the stratosphere the entire time; temperature increased and decreased due to random changes in weather patterns, not layer boundaries
hints: Track which altitude range (0-12, 12-50, 50-85, or 85+) each of the two altitudes (30 and 70 km) falls into.
Each layer has its own temperature trend: remember the pattern is down, up, down, up as you go outward from the ground.

problemText: A student observes that the stratosphere is much warmer at its top (near 50 kilometers) than at its bottom (near 12 kilometers), even though it is higher up. The student incorrectly concludes that 'higher altitude always means warmer temperature in the atmosphere.' Using what you know about the layers and their temperature trends, explain why this conclusion is wrong and give an example from a different layer that contradicts it.
choices: The conclusion is wrong because commercial airplanes fly near the bottom of the stratosphere, proving that temperature must decrease with height everywhere
The conclusion is wrong because the thermosphere is too far away to count as real atmosphere, so the student's rule only works below 85 kilometers
The conclusion is wrong because ozone blocks some sunlight, so the stratosphere does not follow the normal rules that other layers follow
The conclusion is wrong because the mesosphere shows the opposite pattern: it is colder at higher altitudes, contradicting the claim that height always means warmth
hints: Find a layer where temperature gets colder as you go higher, not warmer.
The mesosphere and troposphere both show this opposite trend compared to the stratosphere.

problemText: A satellite orbits Earth at an altitude of 400 kilometers. A student claims that because the satellite is so high up, it must be in the coldest part of the atmosphere. However, scientists who study this region know the student is wrong. Using the four layers, their altitude ranges, and their temperature trends, explain which layer the satellite actually orbits in, why the student's claim is incorrect, and what the actual temperature condition is in this layer compared to the troposphere.
choices: The satellite orbits in the thermosphere; the student incorrectly assumed that higher altitude always means colder temperature, but the thermosphere actually gets warmer at higher altitudes and reaches the hottest temperatures of all four layers

The satellite orbits in the mesosphere; the student did not know that the mesosphere extends only to 85 kilometers, so the satellite is actually above all layers in empty space where temperature cannot be measured

The satellite orbits in the stratosphere; the student confused the stratosphere with the mesosphere, because the stratosphere is where ozone makes it warmer at the top, opposite to what happens in the troposphere

The satellite orbits in the troposphere; the student correctly identified that it would be cold there, but did not realize that the troposphere only extends to about 12 kilometers, so the satellite is actually much higher than this layer
hints: Check which altitude range includes 400 kilometers: Is it 0-12, 12-50, 50-85, or 85+ km?
In the thermosphere, temperature rises with altitude, making it the hottest layer overall even though it is the highest.

problemText: A weather station reports that air pressure at that location has been falling steadily over the past few hours. Based on this pressure trend alone, what is the most likely weather development coming to that station over the next day?
choices: A high-pressure system is approaching, so skies will clear and conditions will become drier.
A low-pressure system is approaching, so clouds and a chance of precipitation are likely to increase.
A warm front has already passed, so temperatures will continue to rise steadily.
No weather change is coming, because pressure trends have no connection to future conditions.
hints: Remember what falling pressure usually signals about the kind of system heading toward a location.
Think about whether falling pressure points toward unsettled conditions or clear skies.

problemText: A weather map shows a cold front drawn as a line running north to south, currently located 80 kilometers west of Westbrook. The front is moving east. Westbrook's station currently reports wind from the south, mild temperature, and partly cloudy skies. Based on the front's type and its direction of travel, what should Westbrook expect as the next major weather change?
choices: A longer period of light, steady rain followed by warmer air.
Skies clearing immediately and temperatures rising over the next several hours.
A brief period of heavier rain or thunderstorms, then a wind shift and cooler, clearer weather.
No significant weather change, because the front is too far away to affect Westbrook yet.
hints: Match the front's type—cold, not warm—to what that type usually produces when it passes through.
Consider both what happens during the front's passage and what arrives afterward.

problemText: Two cities sit on the same weather map. City A has a low-pressure center labeled 120 kilometers to its north, and City A's station reports falling pressure and cloudy skies. City B sits far from any front or pressure center, and City B's station reports rising pressure and clear skies. Based on these readings and the map layout, which city is more likely to receive rain over the next day?
choices: City B, because rising pressure indicates air is sinking and weather systems are moving away from the area.
Neither city, because pressure readings must be combined with wind direction and cloud type before any forecast can be made.
Both cities equally, because they are positioned on the same weather map and experience the same regional pressure patterns.
City A, because the nearby low-pressure center and falling trend both point toward increased clouds and rain.
hints: Notice what a low-pressure center is usually linked to, and then check City A's own pressure trend.
Think about why City B's rising pressure and distance from any system point in a different direction.

problemText: A weather map shows a warm front running east to west, currently positioned about 50 kilometers south of North Station. The front is moving north, directly toward North Station. North Station's current reading shows pressure falling slowly, wind from the southeast, and thin high clouds. South of the front, another station named South Post reports pressure steady, wind from the south, and clear skies. Which statement best describes what North Station and South Post should expect over the next day or two?
choices: North Station will see a longer period of lighter rain as the warm front arrives and moves through, followed by milder air, while South Post, still in the approaching warm air mass, is likely to stay stable and clear for now.

North Station will experience a sudden violent storm with a sharp wind shift and then much colder temperatures, while South Post will warm up gradually as the front passes through and pressure rises steadily.
Both stations will experience the same sequence of weather changes at the same time because they are on opposite sides of the warm front system and will feel its effects simultaneously.
South Post will see rain and wind first because it is south of the front and in the direct path of the warm front's movement toward the north.
hints: Remember that a warm front produces a different pattern of rain and wind than a cold front does.
Consider the position of each station relative to the front and what the already-realized conditions at South Post suggest about what North Station will experience.

problemText: A weather station in Riverside reports falling pressure, wind from the southwest, and increasing cloud cover over the past 6 hours. A meteorologist checks the weather map and finds no front or pressure center marked anywhere near Riverside yet. Based on Riverside's pressure trend alone, what is the most reasonable short-term forecast, and why might the absence of a marked system on the map not contradict that forecast?
choices: Expect continued clear skies and dry conditions, because weather patterns remain stable until a front or pressure center is officially drawn and labeled on the meteorological map.
Expect increasing clouds and a chance of rain to develop over the next day, because the falling pressure suggests a low-pressure system is approaching, even if it has not yet been plotted on the map.

Expect the weather to remain unchanged over the coming days, because pressure trends become reliable only after a front or pressure center is already drawn on the map and identified by meteorologists.
Expect winds to shift from the southwest toward the northeast, because a high-pressure system is pushing into Riverside from that direction and will dominate the pressure pattern.
hints: Think about whether a system's approach must already be drawn on the map before a station can sense its arrival through pressure changes.
Consider the time order: does a station's pressure start to fall only after the front appears on the map, or does the pressure fall first?

problemText: A weather map shows a cold front running north to south, currently positioned 200 kilometers east of Eastville. The front is moving east, away from Eastville. At Eastville, the station reports falling pressure, wind from the south, and partly cloudy skies. Meanwhile, a second city named Frontier sits 80 kilometers east of the cold front; Frontier's station reports steady pressure, wind from the northwest, clear skies, and a cooler temperature than Eastville. Over the next day, a meteorologist must write separate forecasts for both cities. Which forecast pair best matches what the map and readings suggest?
choices: Eastville will experience heavy rain and strong cooling as the cold front moves closer, and Frontier will get warmer air since it is ahead of the front moving east.
Both Eastville and Frontier will experience similar clearing trends because the cold front will eventually reach both cities as it moves east across the region over the next few days.

Eastville's falling pressure needs explanation from a different system, not the cold front moving away; likely a different low-pressure system is approaching Eastville from another direction, bringing increased clouds and rain, while Frontier, already behind the receding front, will stay clear and cool.
Eastville will stay mild and cloudy as a low-pressure system develops there, while Frontier will get storms because it is farther ahead in the path of the receding cold front's movement.
hints: Remember that a front moving away from a city does not cause that city's forecast; a front's direction matters as much as its existence.
Explain Eastville's falling pressure by what system could actually reach it, and use Frontier's already-realized conditions as a clue to the front's influence downstream.

problemText: A cold front is moving into a region where warm, moist air has been sitting for several days. As the front arrives, the cold air moves in low and forces the warm, moist air upward quickly. What type of severe weather is most likely to form as a result of this lifting?
choices: A tornado forming immediately without a thunderstorm first
A hurricane
A thunderstorm
No severe weather, because the two air masses are moving parallel to each other
hints: Recall which severe weather forms when a front lifts warm, moist air quickly.
Think about whether a tornado can form without a thunderstorm developing first.

problemText: A meteorologist is observing a thunderstorm and uses a weather balloon to check the wind at two different heights. Near the ground, the wind is blowing from the south at 10 kilometers per hour. At a height of 5 kilometers, the wind is blowing from the west at 40 kilometers per hour. What does this difference between the two heights represent, and what does it potentially allow to happen inside a strong thunderstorm?
choices: A change in air pressure caused by the altitude difference, which pushes the storm to move in a predictable direction away from towns
A shift in atmospheric stability that occurs when warm air rises, meaning the thunderstorm will gradually lose energy and precipitation will decrease
A stable air mass condition in which temperature stays constant with height, preventing the development of rotating clouds or severe weather phenomena
Wind shear, which can set up a spinning, roughly horizontal tube of air that the storm's updraft may tilt upright into a tornado
hints: Wind shear is a change in wind speed or direction between different heights in the atmosphere.
Think about what a spinning, horizontal tube of air can become if the storm's updraft tilts it upright.

problemText: A large rotating storm system has been spinning over the Atlantic Ocean for three days. It covers an area hundreds of kilometers across. At its center is a calm, mostly cloud-free area, and immediately surrounding that center is a ring of thunderstorms containing the strongest winds and heaviest rain. Based on these characteristics, what type of severe weather is this, and what is the name of that calm central area?
choices: A hurricane, and the calm central area is called the eye
A tornado, and the calm central area is called the pressure zone
A supercell thunderstorm, and the calm central area is called the vortex
A cold front system, and the calm central area is called the stability layer
hints: Which severe weather lasts for days and spans hundreds of kilometers across?
Recall the structure of a hurricane and what the calm center at its core is called.

problemText: A weather forecaster is comparing two storm situations. In Situation 1, a cold front is approaching a warm, moist air mass, and wind speeds increase sharply from the surface to higher altitudes while also changing direction. In Situation 2, warm tropical ocean water is surrounded by low wind shear, and clusters of thunderstorms over the water are organizing together into one larger system. Based on the conditions present, which situation is more likely to produce a tornado, and why?
choices: Situation 2 is more likely to produce a tornado because organized thunderstorms over warm ocean water will eventually develop enough internal rotation to spawn a tornado from the storm's center
Situation 1 is more likely to produce a tornado because the wind shear from the cold front can create a spinning tube of air that a strong thunderstorm's updraft can tilt upright
Both situations are equally likely because each has warm, moist air and thunderstorms present, and these two ingredients alone are sufficient for tornado development to occur
Neither situation is likely to produce a tornado because tornadoes only form from hurricanes, which require sustained winds over 120 kilometers per hour and a completely different atmospheric setup
hints: Wind shear is a key ingredient for tornadoes to form inside thunderstorms; check which situation has clear wind shear.
Recall that a hurricane forms from a single warm air mass without a front, whereas tornadoes are tied to fronts and wind shear.

problemText: A student observes a severe thunderstorm on the ground and hears on the radio that a cold front caused it to develop. The student then asks: 'If a cold front can make a thunderstorm, why doesn't every cold front produce a tornado?' Using what you know about the conditions needed for tornadoes, explain why the student's reasoning is incomplete.
choices: Tornadoes form only when a warm tropical air mass remains over the ocean for extended periods, so cold fronts that occur over land lack the necessary stationary warm water source
Cold fronts actually produce tornadoes every single time they occur, but most tornadoes are too small or weak to be detected by weather instruments and reported by forecasters

A cold front can lift warm, moist air and produce a thunderstorm, but a tornado requires an additional condition: wind shear that sets up a spinning tube of air for the storm's updraft to tilt upright
A cold front by itself generates only scattered light thunderstorms; tornadoes need multiple fronts colliding simultaneously and high atmospheric pressure to create the necessary rotation
hints: Remember that a thunderstorm and a tornado are not the same thing; one is a step beyond the other.
What additional atmospheric ingredient, beyond just a lifting cold front, is needed to turn a thunderstorm into a tornado?

problemText: A hurricane has been sitting over the warm tropical Atlantic Ocean for five days, maintaining its size and strength. Scientists predict that it will weaken significantly once it moves inland over the southeastern United States within 24 hours. A student asks: 'Why can't a hurricane weaken to a regular thunderstorm and then reform as a new hurricane later when it reaches warm water again?' Based on what you know about how hurricanes form and what keeps them organized, explain what the student misunderstands about the conditions hurricanes need.
choices: The student misunderstands that wind shear is actually the main energy source keeping hurricanes organized, so once wind shear decreases over land the system cannot rebuild its structure even if it reaches warm water again
The student is correct that hurricanes can reform; a hurricane that weakens inland and then moves back over warm tropical water will rebuild its organization and regain strength quickly

The student misunderstands that hurricanes are powered by friction between cold and warm frontal boundaries; once this frontal collision ends over land, those collision conditions cannot return even if the hurricane encounters warm water

The student misunderstands that a hurricane requires continuous supply of moisture from warm ocean water and low wind shear to organize many thunderstorms into one large system; once over land it loses that moisture source, and the organized structure falls apart even if it later encounters warm water again
hints: What is the one main energy source that keeps a hurricane's thunderstorms organized into a single large system?
Think about what happens to a hurricane's structure when it moves away from the warm ocean water it depends on.

problemText: An air mass is a large body of air that has been sitting over one region long enough to pick up that region's temperature and moisture. What is the name of the specific stretch of land or ocean where an air mass forms and takes on its characteristics?
choices: source region
front boundary
pressure zone
wind corridor
hints: Think about the starting place where an air mass gets its stamp.
This is the uniform stretch of surface that the air mass sits over for several days.

problemText: Air has been sitting for several days over the frozen tundra of northern Canada, far from any ocean. Based on what kind of surface this is and where it is located, what two properties will this air mass have when it leaves that region and travels south?
choices: warm and humid
cold and dry
warm and dry
cold and humid
hints: Think about the latitude first — is frozen tundra near the equator or near a pole?
Now think about the surface type — does frozen land far from ocean give a steady source of evaporation?

problemText: A cold front is defined as a boundary where an advancing mass of cold air is pushing into and displacing a mass of warmer air that was already there. If you wanted to identify whether a particular moving air boundary is a cold front, which two pieces of information would you need to know first?
choices: whether thunderstorms are happening and how wide the band of rain is
the exact speed of the boundary and how much rain it will produce
the temperature of both air masses and which one is moving in
the humidity of the retreating air and the latitude where the boundary started
hints: The definition of a cold front depends on which air mass is advancing, not on the weather it produces.
You need to know the temperature difference and the direction of motion — that is what makes it a cold front instead of something else.

problemText: A mass of warm, humid air has been sitting over the southern United States for two days. A mass of cold, dry air is now advancing from the north, moving in low and forcing the warm, humid air upward quickly. Based on what happens at a cold front, describe the weather pattern you would expect as this front passes and explain why the pattern would be different if instead a mass of warm, humid air were advancing into the same region while cooler air retreated ahead of it.
choices: The cold front would bring a narrow band of quick, intense showers followed by clearer, cooler air; a warm front would bring light rain because warm air cannot hold snow.

The cold front would bring steady rain for many hours because the boundary moves slowly and warm air rises gradually; a warm front would bring a brief thunderstorm because the boundary moves very fast and forces air upward quickly.

Both would bring the same thunderstorm, but the cold front would happen during the day and the warm front would happen at night because the Earth's rotation affects when fronts arrive and how quickly air is forced upward.

The cold front would bring a narrow band of quick, intense showers followed by clearer, cooler air; a warm front would bring gradual cloud thickening and a longer period of steadier rain followed by warmer, more humid air, because the warm air rises quickly at a cold front but gradually at a warm front.
hints: Remember that at a cold front, the warm air is forced up quickly, and at a warm front, the warm air rises gradually over a slope.
Think about how the speed of that rising air affects whether rain comes in a narrow, quick band or over a longer, wider stretch.

problemText: Two different air masses form over two different regions. Air mass X forms over a warm, dry desert close to the equator. Air mass Y forms over a cool ocean far to the north. Both air masses then travel and keep their temperature and moisture as they move. Which statement correctly compares these two air masses and explains how their source regions produced those differences?
choices: Air mass X is warm and dry; air mass Y is cold and humid. The equatorial desert's low latitude made X warm, while the desert's dry surface made it dry; the northern ocean's high latitude made Y cold, while the ocean surface made it humid.

Air mass X is cold and humid; air mass Y is warm and dry. The temperature of an air mass depends only on the type of surface it forms over, not on the latitude, so desert surfaces always make dry air regardless of location.

Air mass X is warm and humid; air mass Y is cold and dry. Both air masses receive their temperature and moisture properties from the same source region, so locations at opposite latitudes produce opposite conditions for both temperature and moisture.

Both air masses are identical in temperature and moisture because an air mass changes its properties continuously as it travels, making the source region's original characteristics irrelevant to the final result.
hints: Separate the two causes: temperature comes from latitude, and moisture comes from surface type — they are independent.
Check your answer by moving one condition: if the warm desert were at a high latitude instead, would it still be dry? Would it still be warm?

problemText: A weather observer notices that a region has experienced two fronts in the past week. The first front brought a narrow band of intense thunderstorms that lasted only one hour, followed immediately by much cooler, drier air. Four days later, a second front arrived, and this time clouds thickened gradually over several hours, then rain fell steadily for nearly a full day before the air gradually warmed and became more humid. Cold fronts move quickly and force warm air upward rapidly, while warm fronts move slowly and allow warm air to rise gradually. For each front, identify whether it was a cold front or a warm front, and explain how the speed of the front's movement produced the observed weather pattern.
choices: The first was a cold front because the air became cooler immediately afterward and precipitation fell in a narrow band; the second was a warm front because the air became warmer and more humid at the end, with clouds thickening gradually over several hours before steady rain.

The first was a cold front because the warm air was forced upward quickly, producing a narrow, intense band of rain; the second was a warm front because the warm air rose gradually, producing a longer stretch of steadier rain.

Both were cold fronts because both fronts resulted in precipitation and produced measurable changes in temperature and humidity conditions with narrow bands of intense thunderstorms followed by cooler air masses.

The first was a warm front that produced rain over many hours because the slow movement allowed gradual cloud thickening; the second was a cold front that produced intense showers in a narrow band because the rapid upward motion of warm air created severe weather.
hints: Do not use the temperature after the front passes as your clue — use the pattern of rain and how quickly the boundary arrived.
A cold front's boundary moves fast and forces warm air up quickly; a warm front's boundary moves slow and lets warm air rise gradually — these differences in motion produce different rain patterns.
